name: Cross-model agreement scatter with marginals
summary: A scatter where every dot is a matched pair of features from two independently trained models: one axis is the activation correlation used to choose the pair, the other a second, free measure of agreement, with a histogram of each axis along the edges. It is how the paper checks whether two different definitions of “the same feature” agree across a whole population rather than on chosen examples.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Section 5.3.1 asks whether two transformers trained on the same data with different random seeds learn the same [[feature|features]] — the paper's test of [[universality]]. It already has a headline number: the median [[activation-similarity|activation correlation]] between an A/1 feature and its closest partner in run B/1 is $0.72$. What a number cannot settle is whether two different definitions of "the same feature" pick out the same pairs. Two features could fire on the same text and still write something else to the output.

That is a claim about a joint distribution, so it needs a scatter. Two bar charts, or two medians, would give the level of each measure and nothing about the pairing: you could not tell whether the pairs that fire alike are the pairs that predict alike. A table of a few examples invites the charge that they were chosen. And the paper wants the population pattern *and* one pair where the mechanism is legible — a scatter keeps the outlier on the page rather than averaging it away.

### How to read it, step by step

One dot is one matched **pair** of features. Not a token, not a vocabulary entry — this is the trap, because the per-feature comparison scatters earlier in the paper look almost identical and there a dot *is* a datapoint or a vocabulary token. Here each [[sparse-autoencoder]] feature in run A/1 is paired with the B/1 feature it correlates with most, B being the second transformer ([[transformer-a-and-b]]), with its own separately trained dictionary. A/1 holds 4,096 features, so the cloud is a few thousand dots.

The horizontal axis is always activation correlation: the [[pearson-correlation]] between the pair's activation vectors over a fixed set of dataset tokens. It is also the rule used to choose the partner, so every point sits as far right as that A/1 feature can get. Read the bottom marginal as "how good was the best match available", not "how similar are two features in general". It leans right by construction, and is the same histogram in both figures.

The vertical axis is the only free measurement. In fig-53 it is [[logit-weight-similarity]], the correlation of the two [[logit-weight]] vectors indexed by vocabulary. In fig-54 it is [[attribution-similarity]], the correlation of the two [[attribution-vector|attribution vectors]].

Nothing is colour-encoded: both plots are grey, and overplotting density is the only intensity channel. Colour is annotation only — the gold ring on the outlier, the red period label in fig-53's inset. Look first at the diagonal $y = x$; both axes are correlations on the same scale, so it carries meaning. Then read the left marginal: where the free measure piles up, and whether it reaches $1.0$ at all.

### What a bad result would look like

Fig-54 claims attribution correlation tracks activation correlation. Its failure case is a round, untilted blob, or a band pinned near $1.0$ at every $x$, meaning attribution correlation runs high for any pair and measures nothing. A caution the paper does not state: the attribution vector has the activation vector as a factor, so the axes are not independent and some of the diagonal is built in.

Fig-53 is drawn the other way round — it wants a gap, so a tight diagonal would have been its null result. What undercuts its reading is the low points sitting at low $x$ too; then they are bad matches rather than [[weight-interference]] from [[superposition]]. Neither plot can say whether $0.72$ is high; that needs the $0.46$ neuron baseline from the companion histogram.

### Where it comes back

Twice in one subsection, on one population, with the same $x$ and bottom marginal. Only $y$ changes. Fig-53's cloud rises left to right but sags well under the diagonal, its left marginal peaking around $0.5$–$0.6$ and stopping near $0.87$, the axis dipping to $-0.1$ to hold one circled pair. Fig-54's cloud hugs the diagonal and packs into the top-right corner. Read them in order: the second measure is the repair of the first, and the change in cloud shape is the argument. Next door, [[feature-vs-neuron-universality|fig-52]] keeps the same matched pairs, drops the scatter, and shows the horizontal measure alone for features against neurons.
